title: Rabin–Karp Substring Search (Rolling Hash)
directAnswer: Hash the pattern once, then roll a fixed-width hash across the text so each window's hash updates in O(1) instead of recomputing from scratch. When a window's hash equals the pattern's hash, verify character-by-character to rule out a collision (a 'spurious hit'). Average and best case O(n + m); worst case O(n·m) if hashes collide constantly, which a good modulus and base make vanishingly unlikely.

remember.pattern: Rolling polynomial hash over a sliding fixed-width window
remember.formula:
hash(s[0..m-1]) = (s[0]*b^{m-1} + s[1]*b^{m-2} + ... + s[m-1]) mod M
roll forward by one:
    h = ( (h - s[i]*b^{m-1}) * b + s[i+m] ) mod M   (keep non-negative)
on hash match: VERIFY characters before reporting
rules: A hash match is **necessary, not sufficient** — always verify characters to reject spurious hits.
Precompute `b^{m-1} mod M` once; the roll uses it to subtract the outgoing character's contribution.
Pick a **large prime modulus** `M` and a base `b` larger than the alphabet to keep collisions rare.
Take `mod` after every operation and add `M` before another `mod` to keep values non-negative (Java/Python int overflow vs negative quirks differ).
Worst case is `O(n·m)` under adversarial collisions — say this out loud; double-hashing makes it astronomically unlikely.
whenToUse: Substring search where average-case linear time is acceptable
Comparing many equal-length substrings (precomputed hashes give O(1) equality checks)
Detecting duplicate substrings of a fixed length (e.g. Repeated DNA Sequences)
Plagiarism / fingerprinting style problems over sliding windows
antiSignals: You need a guaranteed worst-case linear bound → KMP or Z-algorithm
Tiny inputs where built-in find suffices → don't hand-roll hashing
Adversary controls the input and can engineer collisions → randomize base or use double hashing, or switch to KMP
remember.takeaway: Rabin–Karp trades exactness for speed: a rolling hash compares windows in O(1), and a cheap verification step restores correctness whenever hashes happen to collide. It's the gateway to every rolling-hash / string-fingerprint technique.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you understand that hashing gives a fast probabilistic filter that still needs verification, and whether you can derive the O(1) rolling update with correct modular arithmetic.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reporting a match on hash equality without verifying characters (false positive on a collision), or botching the modular subtraction so values go negative.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the spurious-hit risk explicitly, state the O(n+m) average vs O(n·m) worst case honestly, and mention double hashing as the mitigation.

problemStatement:
Given a text `t` of length `n` and a pattern `p` of length `m`, return **all starting indices** in `t` where `p` occurs, using a rolling hash.

Report overlapping occurrences. Your hash equality must be confirmed by an actual character comparison so that a hash collision never produces a wrong answer.
constraints: Strings are ASCII; treat each character's code as its numeric value
Use a large prime modulus to keep collision probability low
understanding: Comparing the pattern against every window directly costs O(m) per window. Rabin–Karp replaces that with an O(1) hash comparison per window by rolling the hash as the window slides. Because different strings can share a hash, a positive hash test must be confirmed with a real comparison — that confirmation is the heart of getting the answer correct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I have to handle hash collisions?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A matching hash is only a candidate; verify the characters. Skipping verification is a correctness bug, not an optimization.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What modulus and base should I use?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A large prime modulus (e.g. ~10⁹+7) and a base above the alphabet size (e.g. 256 or a random prime). Larger and randomized → fewer collisions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is worst-case O(n·m) acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Average case is O(n+m); worst case degrades only under pathological collisions. If a guaranteed bound is required, use KMP instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Overlapping matches?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the window slides by one each step, so overlaps are reported naturally.

examples.explanation: Windows at 4 and 7 hash equal to p and verify as "abc". Any other coincidental hash matches are rejected by verification.
Overlapping matches; each adjacent window hashes equal and verifies.
No window hash equals p's hash; empty result.

diagrams.title: The two-stage Rabin–Karp filter
diagrams.caption: Hash equality is a fast filter; character verification is the correctness gate that rejects spurious hits.

approaches.name: Naive — Recompute Each Window
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to motivate why an O(1) hash update is worth the modular-arithmetic care.
hints: For each start s from 0 to n−m, compare the window t[s..s+m-1] with p one character at a time.
Each comparison is up to m characters, and there are about n windows → n·m work.
Notice consecutive windows share m−1 characters — recomputing everything ignores that overlap.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Up to n−m+1 windows, each compared in up to m character checks → O(n·m). Constant extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The baseline simply re-derives whether each window equals the pattern from scratch.

**The literal method.** Slide a start index `s` across the text, and at each `s` compare the `m` characters of the window with the pattern. Stop early on the first mismatch; record `s` if all `m` match.

**The overlap it ignores.** Window starting at `s` and window starting at `s+1` share `m−1` characters. The naive method re-reads those shared characters every step. A rolling hash captures the window in a single number so that shifting reuses almost all prior work.

**Worst case.** Text `"aaaa...a"` with pattern `"aaa...ab"` matches `m−1` characters per window before failing — `n` windows × `m` checks ≈ `n·m`. At `n = m = 10⁶` that's 10¹² operations, far too slow.
approaches.insight: The redundancy is the m−1 overlapping characters between adjacent windows. Rabin–Karp's rolling hash is exactly a way to update the window's fingerprint in O(1) instead of rereading that overlap.

dryRun.intro: Compare each window of length 3 with the pattern.

java.line: while (j < m && t.charAt(s + j) == p.charAt(j)) j++;
java.explanation: Re-reads the whole window each shift, ignoring the m−1 shared characters.

python.line: while j < m and t[s + j] == p[j]:
python.explanation: Per-window full comparison — the source of O(n·m).

diagrams.title: Naive windowed comparison
diagrams.caption: Each window is compared from scratch.

pitfalls: Treating it as acceptable at large n — adversarial inputs are genuinely quadratic.
Not early-exiting the inner loop on mismatch (still O(n·m) but slower constant).

approaches.name: Rolling Hash (Optimal Average Case)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Lead with the O(1) hash roll, then immediately address spurious hits and verification.
hints: Treat a length-m string as a base-b number mod M: hash = s[0]*b^{m-1} + ... + s[m-1]. Equal strings always share this hash.
When the window slides one step right, the new hash is (old hash minus the leaving char's high-order term) times b, plus the entering char — an O(1) update if you precompute b^{m-1} mod M.
A matching hash might be a coincidence (collision). Verify the m characters before recording, and you stay correct even when hashes collide.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Computing the pattern hash and the first window hash is O(m). Each of the ~n rolls is O(1). Verifications are O(m) but happen only on hash matches, which are rare with a good modulus → O(n + m) expected. If every window collides (adversarial), every verification costs O(m) → O(n·m) worst case.
approaches.explanation:
Rabin–Karp encodes each fixed-width window as a polynomial hash and slides that hash across the text in constant time per step.

**The hash as a base-b number.** Read the `m` characters of a window as digits of a base-`b` number taken modulo a large prime `M`: `hash = c0·b^{m-1} + c1·b^{m-2} + … + c_{m-1}`. Two windows that are character-for-character equal always produce the same hash. Two different windows usually produce different hashes, but not always — that 'not always' is the collision you must handle.

**The O(1) roll — the core trick.** When the window moves from `[i, i+m-1]` to `[i+1, i+m]`, you want the new hash without recomputing the sum. Subtract the outgoing character's contribution `c_i · b^{m-1}`, multiply the rest by `b` (shifting every digit up one place), then add the incoming character `c_{i+m}`, all mod `M`. Precomputing `b^{m-1} mod M` once makes this three arithmetic operations regardless of `m`.

**Spurious hits and why verification is mandatory.** A hash equal to the pattern's hash is a *candidate*, not a guarantee. Because many strings map into the same residue class mod `M`, two unequal windows can share a hash — a 'spurious hit'. So on every hash match, compare the actual `m` characters. With a large prime `M` and base `b` above the alphabet, spurious hits are rare, so verification rarely fires and the average cost stays linear. But you can never skip it without risking a wrong answer.

**Modular hygiene.** Subtraction can make the intermediate value negative; add `M` before the final `mod` so the stored hash stays in `[0, M)`. In languages with fixed-width integers, also keep the base and modulus small enough that `hash·b` doesn't overflow (use 64-bit, or a modulus near 10⁹).

**Honest complexity.** Average and best case are `O(n + m)`. The worst case is `O(n·m)` when hashes collide on (almost) every window — possible if an adversary engineers the input against a known fixed base/modulus. Randomizing the base or using two independent hashes (double hashing) drives the collision probability to negligible levels.
approaches.insight: A polynomial hash makes 'are these two length-m strings equal?' an O(1) question, and the rolling update makes 'advance the window' O(1) too. The price is that equality becomes probabilistic — so you bolt on a cheap O(m) verification that runs only on the rare hash match, recovering exactness without losing the average-case speed.

dryRun.intro: Compute pattern hash, the first window hash, then roll. On hash equality, verify characters.

java.line: for (int k = 0; k < m - 1; k++) highOrder = (highOrder * BASE) % MOD;
java.explanation: Precompute BASE^(m-1) mod MOD once — the high-order weight removed on each roll.
Horner's method builds the polynomial hash digit by digit.
Hash equality is only a candidate; matches(...) verifies characters to reject spurious hits.

java.line: wHash = (wHash - t.charAt(i) * highOrder % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
java.explanation: Remove the outgoing char's contribution; + MOD keeps the value non-negative after subtraction.
Shift remaining digits up and add the incoming char — the O(1) roll.

python.explanation: Fast modular power for the removed high-order weight.

python.line: if w_hash == p_hash and t[i:i + m] == p:
python.explanation: Verify with a real slice comparison — never trust the hash alone.
Python's % already returns non-negative, so the subtraction is safe here.
Append the entering character to complete the roll.

diagrams.title: Rolling the window hash
diagrams.caption: The outgoing char leaves, the rest shift, the incoming char joins — all in O(1).

pitfalls: Reporting a match on hash equality without verifying characters — wrong on collisions.
Letting the rolling hash go negative after subtraction — add MOD before the final mod (matters in Java).
Integer overflow when MOD·BASE exceeds the type — use 64-bit and a modulus near 10⁹.
Using a tiny modulus 'to keep numbers small' — collisions become frequent and you drift toward O(n·m).

edgeCases.behavior: Adjacent windows all hash equal and verify → overlapping matches [0,1,2,3].
Verification still keeps the answer correct; only the time degrades toward O(n·m). Double hashing mitigates.

commonMistakes: Skipping character verification and trusting hash equality — false positives on collisions.
Modular subtraction producing a negative hash because + MOD was omitted.
Choosing a small modulus that makes spurious hits common and degrades performance.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No verification after a hash match
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Different strings can share a hash (spurious hit). Reporting on hash equality alone returns wrong indices whenever a collision occurs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if w_hash == p_hash:
    result.append(i)   # WRONG: collision => false positive
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if w_hash == p_hash and t[i:i + m] == p:
    result.append(i)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Negative hash after the roll
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In fixed-width-int languages, subtracting the outgoing term can make the hash negative, corrupting later comparisons. Add MOD before taking mod again.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: wHash = (wHash - t.charAt(i) * highOrder % MOD) % MOD; // may be negative
commonMistakesDetailed.good: wHash = (wHash - t.charAt(i) * highOrder % MOD + MOD) % MOD;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Modulus too small
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A small M means many strings collide, so verification fires constantly and the algorithm slides toward its O(n·m) worst case while also risking overflow-free but useless hashes.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: MOD = 1_000_000_007   # large prime keeps spurious hits rare

followupVariations.title: Repeated DNA Sequences
followupVariations.hint: Roll a fixed-length (10) hash and bucket windows to find sequences appearing more than once.

followupVariations.title: Longest Duplicate Substring
followupVariations.hint: Binary search the length, use rolling hashes (double-hashed) to test for a repeated substring of that length.

followupVariations.title: Find All Anagram Hashes
followupVariations.hint: Use a frequency-based rolling signature instead of a positional polynomial hash.

followupVariations.title: KMP / Z (guaranteed worst case)
followupVariations.hint: When you must avoid the O(n·m) collision worst case entirely, switch to a comparison-based linear matcher.

patternNote: Rolling Hash / String Fingerprinting. Recognise it whenever you slide a fixed-width window and need fast equality: substring search, duplicate-substring detection, and longest-duplicate-via-binary-search all ride on the O(1) rolling update plus verification.
